claim: Scaled content abuse is many pages made mainly to manipulate rankings, however they are made
exact_words: Scaled content abuse is when many pages are generated for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings and not helping users. This abusive practice is typically focused on creating large amounts of unoriginal content that provides little to no value to users, no matter how it's created.

claim: Keyword-bearing pages that make little sense to a reader are a named example of scaled abuse
exact_words: Creating many pages where the content makes little or no sense to a reader but contains search keywords

claim: Doorways are pages made to rank for similar queries that lead to a less useful intermediate page
exact_words: Doorway abuse is when sites or pages are created to rank for specific, similar search queries. They lead users to intermediate pages that aren't as useful as the final destination.

claim: A page that funnels the visitor to the usable part of the site elsewhere is a doorway
exact_words: Generating pages to funnel visitors into the actual usable or relevant portion of a site

claim: Near-duplicate pages outside a browsable hierarchy are a doorway sign; a hierarchy is the remedy the wording implies
exact_words: Creating substantially similar pages that are closer to search results than a clearly defined, browseable hierarchy

exact_words: Last updated 2026-08-28 UTC.

claim: Google asks whether a page adds substantial value over the other results
exact_words: Does the content provide substantial value when compared to other pages in search results?

claim: Google has no preferred word count
exact_words: Are you writing to a particular word count because you've heard or read that Google has a preferred word count? (No, we don't.)

claim: Extensive automation across many topics is a warning sign
exact_words: Are you using extensive automation to produce content on many topics?

claim: A page that leaves the reader needing to search again is a warning sign
exact_words: Does your content leave readers feeling like they need to search again to get better information from other sources?

claim: Clear sourcing is named as a trust signal
exact_words: Does the content present information in a way that makes you want to trust it, such as clear sourcing, evidence of the expertise involved, background about the author or the site that publishes it

claim: Easily verified factual errors count against a page

exact_words: ensuring that we can take action on scaled content abuse as needed, no matter whether content is produced through automation, human efforts, or some combination of human and automated processes.
